mark_split.label: Divide, then set up the form

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Senior Inter Maths-2A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.68 — SAQ chapter 11 Partial Fractions, answer 103. Printed appearances: none — this answer carries no year tag. ⚠ THE 1+1+1+1 SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — this chapter prints no [N Marks] tags against any answer, only tick boxes. The split is the four moves of the method (set up the form · clear the denominators · find the constants · write the result), one mark each, and the SAME split and the SAME step ids (s1_form, s2_identity, s3_constants, s4_result) are used on all fifteen cards of this unit, deliberately: they are one method over different fractions. For the improper fractions the division lives inside s1_form, and for the (x − 3)³ question the substitution x − 3 = y takes the place of the form. The book's SAQ chapter header carries ★★★ and reads '4 Marks'; that star is the CHAPTER's rank, not this question's. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Paper position: Maths-2A Section B runs Q11–Q17 at 4 marks each, answer any 5 of 7; Q15 is the Partial Fractions slot (the chapter has no Section A or Section C slot). Not asked at Q15 in any of the five model papers. No two-book check and no board back-test exist for this paper — recorded, not hidden. A back-test against the book's own six papers (the five Model Guess Papers plus the Bullet Model Paper, 199 slot-instances) WAS run on 2026-08-29: all 199 resolved to an authored card, and every one carried the section and marks its slot implies. That is a substitute corpus, not a board paper — it cannot show what the board asks that this book omits. The book multiplies its identity through by 2 (2x³ = (2x − 1)(x − 1)² + 2A(x − 1)² + …) to avoid the 1/2; the card keeps the plain identity x³ = (1/2)(2x − 1)(x − 1)² + A(x − 1)² + B(2x − 1)(x − 1) + C(2x − 1), which gives the same A = 1/2, B = 1, C = 1. Both are correct. Truth check: putting x = 2 in the identity gives 8 = (1/2)(3)(1) + A(1) + B(3)(1) + C(3) = 3/2 + 1/2 + 3 + 3 = 8 with A = 1/2, B = 1, C = 1.

recall_prompt: Say how you would resolve x³/((2x − 1)(x − 1)²) into partial fractions — name each move in order, starting with what must be done before the form is written.
insider_note: The fraction is improper, so the constant 1/2 from the leading coefficients 1 and 2 must stand in front of the form; and the substitution for A uses x = 1/2, the root of 2x − 1, not x = 1.

steps.label: Divide, then set up the form
steps.margin_note: First mark. Degree 3 on top, degree 3 below: improper, but the quotient is only a constant, the ratio of the leading coefficients 1/2. So write 1/2 plus the usual form for (2x − 1)(x − 1)²: A over (2x − 1), B over (x − 1), C over (x − 1)².

recall.must_convey: That equal degrees make the quotient the constant 1/2, and the form is 1/2 + A/(2x − 1) + B/(x − 1) + C/(x − 1)² with two fractions for the repeated factor.
accept: the degrees are equal so the quotient is the constant half, then write half plus A over two x minus one plus B over x minus one plus C over x minus one squared
improper with equal degrees so a constant half comes first and the repeated factor gives two fractions
half plus A by 2x minus 1 plus B by x minus 1 plus C by x minus 1 whole square
degrees same kabatti quotient half, tarvata A by two x minus one plus B by x minus one plus C by x minus one square rasali
write the constant from the leading coefficients and then one fraction for two x minus one and two for the repeated x minus one
heard_as: A over two x minus one
C over x minus one squared

steps.why: When numerator and denominator have the same degree, dividing gives a constant quotient equal to the ratio of the leading coefficients, x³ over 2x³, and a remainder of lower degree. That constant must be written before the form, or no A, B, C can satisfy the identity.
common_mistakes: Writing A/(2x − 1) + B/(x − 1) + C/(x − 1)² with no 1/2 in front.
Writing the constant as 2 instead of 1/2.
Missing the B/(x − 1) fraction for the repeated factor.

steps.label: Clear the denominators
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Multiply by (2x − 1)(x − 1)². The 1/2 keeps the whole denominator, A keeps (x − 1)², B keeps (2x − 1)(x − 1), C keeps (2x − 1).

recall.must_convey: That multiplying through gives x³ = (1/2)(2x − 1)(x − 1)² + A(x − 1)² + B(2x − 1)(x − 1) + C(2x − 1).
accept: multiply both sides by two x minus one into x minus one squared to get x cubed equals half into the whole denominator plus A into x minus one squared plus B into two x minus one into x minus one plus C into two x minus one
clear the denominators and the half keeps the whole denominator as a term
x cubed equals half times two x minus one times x minus one squared plus A x minus one squared plus B two x minus one x minus one plus C two x minus one
denominator tho multiply cheste x cube equals half into whole denominator plus A into x minus one square plus B into two x minus one x minus one plus C into two x minus one
remove the fractions and keep the half term multiplied by the full denominator
heard_as: A into x minus one squared
B into two x minus one
C into two x minus one

steps.why: The constant 1/2 is a term of the equation, so it too gets multiplied by the denominator. Forgetting that term is the same error as forgetting the quotient in a long-division question.
common_mistakes: Giving C the factor (x − 1) instead of (2x − 1).
Giving B the factor (x − 1)² instead of (2x − 1)(x − 1).

steps.label: Find the constants
steps.margin_note: Third mark. x = 1/2 makes every term except A zero: 1/8 = A/4. x = 1 leaves only C: 1 = C. Then x = 0 gives one equation in A, B, C, which is B once A and C are known.

recall.must_convey: That x = 1/2 gives A = 1/2, x = 1 gives C = 1, and x = 0 gives 0 = −1/2 + A + B − C, so B = 1.
accept: put x equals half to get A equals half, x equals one to get C equals one, then x equals zero to get zero equals minus half plus A plus B minus C so B is one
the two roots half and one give A half and C one, and x equals zero gives B one
A half, C one, B one
x equals half pedithe A half, x equals one pedithe C one, x equals zero pedithe B one vastundi
two roots and one extra value give the three constants

steps.why: The root of 2x − 1 is x = 1/2, not x = 1 or x = 2. It makes (2x − 1) zero in every term but A. x = 1 does the same for C. B has no root of its own, so any third value, x = 0 being the easiest, gives the last equation.
common_mistakes: Using x = 1 for the factor (2x − 1); its root is x = 1/2.
Computing (1/2 − 1)² as 1/2 instead of 1/4, which makes A come out as 1/4.
At x = 0 writing (1/2)(−1)(1) as +1/2 instead of −1/2, giving B = 0.

steps.label: Write the result
steps.margin_note: Last mark. The constant 1/2 comes first, then A = 1/2 over (2x − 1) becomes 1/(2(2x − 1)), then 1/(x − 1) and 1/(x − 1)². Four terms; the result is too long for one box, so the constants are boxed under it.

lines.text: ∴ A = 1/2, B = 1, C = 1 in the form above

recall.must_convey: That the fraction equals 1/2 + 1/(2(2x − 1)) + 1/(x − 1) + 1/(x − 1)², with the constant 1/2 in front.

steps.why: The constant quotient is part of the answer, exactly as a polynomial quotient would be. All four terms, in the form set up in step 1, are what the examiner marks.
common_mistakes: Leaving out the 1/2 in the final line.
Writing 1/2(2x − 1) so it reads as half times the bracket; put the 2 inside the denominator bracket.
Not checking: put x = 2 in the identity, 8 = 3/2 + 1/2 + 3 + 3. If the two sides differ, a constant is wrong.
